actSpeakBrief: Argue aloud first. Concede one point before you attack it.
actSpeak1: Your partner says cutting emissions is a job for governments, not individuals. Take the other side — and grant them their best point first.
actSpeak2: Defend free hospital treatment for everyone to a partner who thinks heavy smokers should pay. Set your limit with "provided that".
actSpeak3: Now argue the side you actually disagree with, well enough that your partner cannot tell.
actWriteBrief: Some people believe individuals should be responsible for cutting their own carbon emissions; others argue this is a job for governments alone. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
actPlaceholder: Introduction: reframe the question, then state your view…
coverSub: Two band 9 essays taken apart move by move — then the same two questions answered badly
s2Title: How to read a model answer
s2A: Read for the moves, not the words. Every paragraph below is doing a job. Learn the job and you can do it on any topic; learn the sentence and you can only do it on this one.
s2B: Do not memorise phrases. An examiner has read "in this modern era" ten thousand times, and a memorised opening scores nothing at all — it is treated as words you did not write.
s2Note: Each essay here comes twice: once at band 9, once at around band 6. The gap between them is where the marks are.
s3A: Task response. Did you answer the question that was asked, take a clear position, and support it? This is where most answers are lost.
s3B: Coherence and cohesion. Does the essay move in a straight line, and do the joins between ideas feel necessary rather than decorative?
s3C: Lexical resource. Range and precision — not long words. The right ordinary word beats the wrong impressive one every time.
s3D: Grammatical range and accuracy. A mix of structures, controlled. Simple sentences are fine; an essay built only from simple sentences is not.
s4Title: Read the task before you read the model
s4A: "To what extent" is an instruction to commit. Fully, partly, or not at all — but say which, in the introduction, and hold it to the end.
s4B: The topic is who decides, not whether home working is good. An essay listing the benefits of working from home has answered a different question.
s5A: Sentence 1 — paraphrase. The task is restated in the writer's own words. Not one phrase is lifted from the question paper.
s5B: Sentence 2 — position, with its limit. "Provided that" plants the condition the whole essay will go on to defend.
s6Title: Why state your view this early?
s7Title: One claim, then evidence for it
s7A: Topic sentence. One claim, stated first, and the rest of the paragraph never leaves it.
s7B: Two specific people — not "many people". The contrast between them is the argument, not decoration around it.
s8Title: Argue against yourself, then resolve it
s8A: Concession, then resolution. The limit promised by "provided that" in the introduction is now argued and settled — the essay does not sit on the fence, it moves through the objection and comes out the other side still holding its position.
s10A: Same position, condition intact. "Primarily" and "only within limits" carry the whole essay in four words.
s10B: No new argument. The last line sharpens what was already proved. A fresh idea here costs marks rather than earning them.
s11Title: The same task at band 6, shortened
s11A: Three problems already. "In this modern era" is memorised filler. "I will discuss both the advantages and the disadvantages" announces the wrong essay type — the task asked how far the writer agrees. And pollution is not what the question is about.
s12Title: It gets worse at the end
s12A: The position arrives in the last line, and contradicts the line before it. "It depends on the person" — then the decision is handed to the company. Note also the four linkers doing no work: Firstly, Secondly, Moreover, Furthermore.
s14Title: Match the fault to what it costs
s14Ctx: Click a term on the left, then the symptom on the right that an examiner would mark it for.
s15Title: A discussion essay has three jobs
s15A: Both views, fairly. Each side gets a paragraph and its best argument, not a straw man built to be knocked down.
s15B: And your own opinion — a third job, not an optional extra. Omit it and the answer cannot reach band 6 for task response.
s16Title: Say where you stand before you discuss
s16A: The question reframed as a choice between two payers — sharper than the original wording, and not copied from it.
s16B: The opinion is already here. The two body paragraphs are then read as the reasoning behind a view the examiner already knows.
s17A: "Those who argue" marks it as reported, not owned. The paragraph then gives the view its two best arguments — public return and access — and does not undercut either one. Presenting a view fairly is what "discuss" means.
s18Title: View two, given the same respect
s18A: Equal length, equal seriousness. The writer rejects full fees and still gives this view its two best arguments. A reader cannot yet tell which side the essay will land on — and that is correct at this point.
s20Title: An opinion built from both views
s20A: Not a compromise for its own sake. It names which principle it takes from each side and why that combination survives both.
s20B: Nothing new enters. Every idea in this paragraph was argued above. The conclusion only decides between them.
s21Title: Where the weaker answer loses it
s21A: The opinion arrives late and from nowhere. Taxing the wealthy was not one of the two views under discussion, so the conclusion decides a question the essay never argued — and "everybody will be happy" is a claim no examiner can credit.
s22Title: It has an opinion. Why is it still weak?
s23Title: Owning a view, and conceding one
s24Title: Reporting a view, and settling it
x07a: Task response asks for a clear position throughout the answer. If it surfaces only in the conclusion, most of the essay has been read without it.
x07b: Length is not the issue. A position placed late is not repetitive — it is simply missing from the paragraphs that needed it.
x07c: There is no fixed sentence in which a thesis must appear. What matters is that the reader knows the view before the arguments begin.
x07d: Paraphrasing first is conventional but it is not a rule, and it is not why an early position helps. The reason is that the body paragraphs need it.
x07e: A clear position, stated early and held, is the single biggest lever on task response.
x10a: Balance for its own sake is not rewarded, and an essay that gives equal weight to both sides without deciding actually loses marks for position.
x10b: It does not. The final paragraph holds the same position as the first — the concession narrows the claim, it does not replace it.
x10c: A position that has survived an objection is a supported position. That is exactly what task response rewards.
x10d: There is no required number of paragraphs. Three or five can both reach band 9 if each one does a job.
x10e: Concede, then resolve. Concede and stop, and you have written a fence-sitting answer.
x14a: Simple linkers are a symptom here, not the cause. Even with elegant cohesion this answer would still be addressing the wrong question.
x14b: It answers “what are the advantages and disadvantages” — a question the paper did not ask. Nothing else can repair that, however well written the rest is.
x14c: The opposite is true — it has no developed examples at all. But the deeper fault is the question it chose to answer.
x14d: The register is impersonal and acceptable throughout. Informality is not what is costing this answer its marks.
x14e: Task response is a quarter of the score, and answering the wrong question caps it however well the rest is written.
x15a: Every one of these is visible in the band 6 answer you have just read.
x20a: Count them — the two paragraphs are almost exactly the same length, and deliberately so. Weighting by word count is not how a position is signalled.
x20b: There is none. “Essentially one of fairness” is respectful, and loaded language against a view you must discuss costs marks.
x20c: Order carries no meaning. Either view can come first; what matters is that the writer's own position is stated somewhere clear.
x20d: Stated in the introduction, confirmed in the conclusion. The body paragraphs stay neutral precisely because the frame around them is not.
x20e: Discuss both views neutrally in the body; carry your own position in the introduction and conclusion.
x23a: Strong opinions are fine and often score well. The problem is that this one is unconnected to the body of the essay, not that it is firm.
x23b: The first person is fine in Task 2 — in my opinion is expected. The fault is where this opinion comes from, not how it is phrased.
x23c: An opinion has to be the conclusion of the discussion, not a fresh topic introduced after it. Otherwise the two views were never really discussed at all.
x23d: It does not repeat either view — that is precisely the trouble. It introduces a third idea and calls it a conclusion.
x23e: Your opinion must be visible in the introduction and settled by the conclusion, built out of what you discussed.
x24a: In my view — the introduction. It cannot be mistaken for reporting somebody else’s opinion.
x24b: However, mid-sentence — the concession. After the comma it reads as an argument turning, not a linker bolted to the front.
x25a: Those who argue — the body of a discussion essay. It reports a view without the writer adopting it.
x25b: Therefore — the conclusion. It claims the paragraphs above have earned this, which an unargued essay cannot honestly do.
